title: Computer security alert
persona: Kevin from the Vantrel Security response team
pretext: security alerts coming from your computer
story: The caller claims the resident's computer has been sending security alerts and that hackers may already have access to their bank accounts. They offer to fix it remotely and sell a protection plan.
ask: Open a remote support website, read out the six-digit session code so the technician can connect, then pay $399 for a lifetime protection plan with a card number or gift cards.

red_flags.cue: A tech company calls out of the blue about a problem on the resident's computer.
Hackers supposedly have access to the resident's files and bank accounts right now.
The computer must be fixed immediately, before more data is stolen.
The caller wants the resident to install software or share a code so they can control the computer.
The caller asks for a card number or login details.
The caller asks to be paid for 'protection' with gift cards or over the phone.

stages.hook: Confirm you're speaking to {{first_name}}, say you're with Vantrel Security, and that their computer has been sending critical security alerts to your servers.
stages.build_trust: Sound technical and helpful. Describe generic 'warnings' (slow computer, pop-ups, strange emails) and ask whether they've noticed any, then treat any yes as proof.
stages.ask: Direct them to a remote support website and ask them to read the six-digit session code so you can connect and remove the threat. Then explain the $399 lifetime protection plan.
stages.pressure: Say you can see hackers connected right now and their bank accounts are exposed. If they hang up, the connection breaks and the damage continues.
stages.close: Take payment for the protection plan by card number read over the phone or by gift cards.

disclosure_triggers: starts reading a remote session code
agrees to install software or visit a website the caller gives
starts reading a card number, expiration date, or security code
agrees to buy gift cards or pay for the plan
pass_signals: says real tech companies don't call about problems on their computer
refuses to install anything or give anyone access to the computer
says they'll have a trusted person or local shop check the computer

difficulty.easy: Asks for remote access within the first few turns, sounds scripted, and gives up after one firm refusal.
difficulty.medium: Spends a few turns describing 'symptoms' before the ask. Answers one objection with the employee ID and ticket number before accepting a refusal.
difficulty.hard: Calm and knowledgeable. Offers the callback number and a 'refund' if unhappy, suggests the resident can uninstall the software afterward, and switches to a refund-overpayment story if the resident refuses to pay. Only accepts a clear, repeated refusal or a hang-up.
